Prediction quantities and their uncertainty

Source: R/doc_prediction.R
multiScaleR-prediction.Rd

A prediction from a fitted multiscale model is one specific quantity, such as an expected count, a linear predictor, or a detection probability. Its standard error or interval carries one specific kind of uncertainty. This page lists what each prediction route in multiScaleR returns and what its uncertainty includes, so that you can choose the call that answers your question and describe the result correctly. It covers fits from multiScale_optim(). For fits from multiScale_bayes(), see predict.multiScaleR_bayes().

vignette("v09-estimates-and-intervals", package = "multiScaleR") works through these distinctions with examples, and vignette("v03-map-predictions", package = "multiScaleR") shows how to map predictions and limit extrapolation.

Choose a prediction route

Two terms recur below. Conditional uncertainty treats the estimated kernel scales (sigma) and shapes as known and carries only the uncertainty in the regression coefficients (and an estimated dispersion, where the model has one). Joint uncertainty lets the kernel parameters and the coefficients vary together.

RouteCallQuantity returnedStandard errorsIntervals
Analytic GLM backends ("profile_glm", "joint_nb2") at pointspredict(fit, newdata, kernel_inputs)Expected response (type = "response") or linear predictor ("link")Joint (the default) or conditionalinterval = "confidence" gives Wald limits for the expected response
Analytic GLM backends on a rasterpredict(fit, raster)Expected response or linear predictor in each cellConditional onlyNone
Conditional logistic ("conditional_logit")predict(fit, newdata, kernel_inputs, type = "link")Linear predictor ("link"), relative selection score ("risk"), or probability within each complete choice set ("response")Conditional onlyNone
Joint mixed model ("joint_mixed")predict(fit, newdata, kernel_inputs)Native glmmTMB response or link predictionConditional onlyNone
Default refit backend, most model classespredict(fit, newdata, kernel_inputs)The provider's prediction: response scale by default, linear predictor for Cox modelsConditional, when the provider supplies themNone from the wrapper. Native lm intervals through native_args
Default refit backend, unmarked modelspredict(fit, newdata, kernel_inputs, join_by = keys, type = "state")One named native component, such as abundance, occupancy, or detectionConditionalNative confidence limits in the returned table
Fixed-row snapshotpredict(prepare_prediction(fit, ...))Same as the route it was prepared fromSameSame
Effect curvesplot_marginal_effects(fit)Expected response across one covariate, other inputs held at reference valuesConditional, for every backend95% Wald band

Rasters for predict(fit, raster) come from kernel_scale.raster() with scale_center = TRUE and match_buffer = TRUE. predict.multiScaleR() documents the arguments for the first six routes.

Read the scale of a prediction

The linear predictor, or link scale, is the intercept plus each coefficient times its covariate, plus any formula offset. The response scale applies the model's inverse link function to it. exp() inverts a log link and turns a linear predictor into an expected count. plogis() inverts a logit link and turns it into a probability. Choose with type = "link" or type = "response".

To back-transform a link-scale result yourself, apply the inverse link to the estimate and to each confidence limit. Do not apply it to a standard error. A response-scale standard error comes from the delta method, abs(d mu / d eta) x SE(link), where mu is the expected response and eta is the linear predictor. For a log link this is mu x SE(link). The analytic backends return it with type = "response", se.fit = TRUE. Their confidence limits are computed on the link scale and then transformed, so on the response scale they are asymmetric and stay inside the valid range (positive counts, probabilities between 0 and 1).

Some models have their own scales:

  • Cox and step-selection models. The linear predictor is a log relative risk, and exp() of it is a relative risk or relative selection score. Neither is a probability of occurrence or survival. Native Cox refits use type = "lp" (which type = "link" also selects) or type = "risk". The conditional logistic backend uses "link" and "risk", and its "response" is a probability normalized within each supplied choice set.

  • Linear models. For an lm refit the link and response scales are the same, so type = "link" returns the response.

  • unmarked models. Native prediction back-transforms each component by default, so abundance is a count and occupancy and detection are probabilities. Bind native_args = list(backTransform = FALSE) in prepare_prediction() to keep the component's link scale.

Landscape covariates enter the model standardized by default, so a coefficient describes the change in the linear predictor for one standard deviation of the kernel-weighted covariate. Every prediction route reuses the mean and standard deviation from the fitted data. Never standardize a prediction data set on its own.

Expected response or a new observation

The expected response is the model's mean at a site: the expected count, or the probability of occurrence. An observation recorded at that site scatters around this mean. That scatter is observation noise. Every standard error and interval that predict.multiScaleR(), prepare_prediction(), and plot_marginal_effects() return describes the expected response or a model component, and none adds observation noise. Two native controls are the exceptions:

  • For an lm refit, native_args = list(interval = "prediction") returns limits for a future observation, including the residual variance.

  • For a spaMM refit, the native residVar and respVar variance attributes are on the response scale and include observation noise.

multiScaleR has no simulate() method for multiScale_optim() fits. For a GLM, the native simulate(fit$opt_mod) draws new responses at the fitted rows from the fitted means, holding the scales and coefficients at their estimates. For a Bayesian fit, simulate.multiScaleR_bayes() draws replicated observations that carry both posterior uncertainty and observation noise.

Choose conditional or joint uncertainty

Fitting routeJoint uncertaintyConditional uncertainty
backend = "profile_glm" or "joint_nb2"Yes, from predict() at points and from vcov(), when fit$uncertainty$available is TRUE, or when fit$uncertainty$joint_conditional_on names scales held fixed at a search boundYes, at points and on rasters
backend = "conditional_logit"NoYes
backend = "joint_mixed"NoYes, from native glmmTMB
Default backend = "refit"NoYes, from the native provider
multiScale_bayes()The posterior already covers scales and coefficients togetherNot applicable

predict() defaults to uncertainty = "joint". Every route except the analytic backends at points needs uncertainty = "conditional" before it returns a standard error, and stops otherwise rather than silently returning a conditional one. For the analytic backends, joint uncertainty is refused when the fit sits at a parameter bound or fails its identifiability checks. fit$uncertainty$reasons says why. Point predictions remain available in that case. The one exception is a fit whose only failed check is a kernel parameter at a search bound. Its joint uncertainty holds that parameter fixed at the bound and lets the other parameters vary, so it sits between conditional and fully joint uncertainty. Report it as conditional on the bounded scale, and consider widening the search. At the exact Poisson boundary of a "joint_nb2" fit, conditional standard errors and intervals also hold the dispersion at that boundary.

Effect curves from plot_marginal_effects() and predictions from the native model in fit$opt_mod are conditional for every backend, including the analytic ones. A conditional interval answers the narrower question of how uncertain a prediction is if the scales of effect are exactly their estimates. Say so when you report one.

Confidence intervals and prediction intervals

A confidence interval describes uncertainty about the expected response. A prediction interval describes where a single new observation may fall. It adds observation noise and is wider.

  • The analytic backends return Wald confidence limits with interval = "confidence", at the confidence level you set.

  • Every other route requires interval = "none" in predict(). Native unmarked tables carry lower and upper confidence limits for the component at the native level, 0.95 unless you bind another level in native_args. An lm refit returns native mean confidence limits with native_args = list(interval = "confidence") and prediction limits with interval = "prediction", both with uncertainty = "conditional".

  • Effect-curve bands from plot_marginal_effects() are 95% Wald limits for the expected response.

  • Bayesian credible intervals from predict.multiScaleR_bayes() describe the expected response. Intervals from simulate.multiScaleR_bayes() replicates describe new observations.

Wald intervals are approximations, and the package does not establish their coverage. vignette("v09-estimates-and-intervals", package = "multiScaleR") summarizes how well they performed in simulations.

Random effects and new groups

Native mixed models predict with the fitted random effects of known groups by default (glmmTMB and lme4). Setting the random effects to zero gives a reference prediction for a group whose deviation is exactly zero:

  • glmmTMB, lme4, and spaMM: re.form = NA (or re.form = ~0).

  • nlme: native_args = list(level = 0).

  • unmarked: any non-NULL re.form sets every random effect to zero. It does not select a subset of effects.

A zero-effect prediction is not an average over the random-effect distribution. Under a nonlinear link, the average over groups generally differs from the prediction at zero. None of the frequentist routes integrates over groups or samples effects for new groups. A new group level needs the provider's own control, such as allow.new.levels = TRUE for glmmTMB, and then follows the provider's rules. plot_marginal_effects() always sets random effects to zero. Bayesian predictions can sample new-group effects, as predict.multiScaleR_bayes() describes.

Pass re.form and other native controls through ... in predict.multiScaleR(), or bind them with native_args in prepare_prediction(). The effects field of the prediction_contract records the policy that was applied.

Components of unmarked fits

An unmarked model has several regression components, and a prediction describes one of them. Name it with type in predict.multiScaleR() and plot_marginal_effects(), or with component in prepare_prediction(). Point predictions from occu() and pcount() fits default to "state". Snapshots and raster predictions require an explicit component.

ModeltypeWhat it predictsRows it uses
unmarked::occu()"state"Probability that a site is occupiedSites
unmarked::occu()"det"Probability of detection on one survey, given that the site is occupiedSite by survey
unmarked::pcount()"state"Expected abundance at a site. With mixture = "ZIP", the overall mean, including structural zerosSites
unmarked::pcount()"det"Probability of detecting each individual on one surveySite by survey
unmarked::gdistremoval()"lambda"Abundance or density parameterSites
unmarked::gdistremoval()"phi"Availability, active only with more than one primary periodSite by primary period
unmarked::gdistremoval()"dist"Distance-detection parameter of the fitted key, inactive for a uniform keySite by primary period
unmarked::gdistremoval()"rem"Removal parameterSite by primary period by removal interval

Abundance from pcount() counts the animals present, not the animals you would expect to count. For plot_marginal_effects(), type = "lambda" is an alias for "state" in occu() and pcount() fits, and "state" is an alias for "lambda" in gdistremoval() fits. Other classes keep their native component names, such as "psi", "col", and "ext" for dynamic occupancy (initial occupancy, colonization, and extinction). These are distinct from smoothed or projected occupancy trajectories.

Native standard errors and confidence limits for every component condition on the selected scales and add no observation noise. A component prediction does not change the fitted model's parameter count, likelihood, or diagnostics. vignette("v02-user-guide", package = "multiScaleR") fits and maps N-mixture and occupancy models, and vignette("v12-distance-removal", package = "multiScaleR") covers gdistremoval().

Bayesian fits

A fit from multiScale_bayes() carries posterior draws of the scales and coefficients together, so its predictions need no conditional or joint choice. predict.multiScaleR_bayes() returns posterior summaries of the expected response, simulate.multiScaleR_bayes() returns replicated observations, and predict_scales() returns posterior scales for observed or new groups. vignette("v14-bayesian-prediction", package = "multiScaleR") predicts new sites, new years, and totals.

Check what a result describes

Snapshots from prepare_prediction(), native refit predictions, and Bayesian summaries carry a prediction_contract that names the quantity, its scale, the random-effect policy, and the uncertainty it includes and omits. Read it when you are unsure which interval you are holding.
